Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal

PCP (phencyclidine) and stimulants · opioids · alcohol withdrawal · benzodiazepines · cannabisWhich drug do the pupils and vital signs point to, and is it intoxication or withdrawal?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Pinpoint pupils slow breathing decreased consciousness: opioid; give naloxone, with bag-mask breaths meanwhile
  • Agitation from PCP (phencyclidine), cocaine or amphetamine: treat with a benzodiazepine; no beta-blocker for cocaine
  • Alcohol withdrawal (delirium tremens, usually at 48 to 96 h) and benzodiazepine withdrawal can kill: a benzodiazepine, thiamine before glucose; taper a benzodiazepine, never stop it abruptly
What it is

Intoxication: a toxidrome read from pupils breathing vital signs

Withdrawal: timed from the last dose

Driver

Stimulants: sympathomimetic surge

Opioids: act at opioid receptors MechanismNaloxone is a competitive antagonist there.

Sedative withdrawal: onset and length follow half-life duration of use

Triggers

Stopping alcohol withdrawal, timed from the last drink (step 5)

Stopping a benzodiazepine abruptly withdrawal, which can be life-threatening

Intravenous glucose before thiamine Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, nystagmus or eye-muscle palsy, ataxia)

Chain

Alcohol stopped tremor, anxiety hallucinosis or seizures delirium tremens

PCP: psychomotor agitation hyperthermia

Cocaine: hemodynamic surge vasoconstriction acute coronary syndrome

Insights

Dilated pupils with autonomic overactivity fit a stimulant and opioid withdrawal alike; yawning and goose flesh mark withdrawal

Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can kill; a spontaneous opioid stop is distressing, not life-threatening

Substance by substancedetail behind the chain
PCPNystagmus (horizontal, vertical or rotary) in 60% to 90%; hypertension in 60%, tachycardia in 30%Complications: rhabdomyolysis, hypoglycemia, seizures, hypertensive crisis, coma
StimulantComplications: seizures, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, coronary or cerebral ischemia
Opioid withdrawalTearing, runny nose, goose flesh, muscle aches, diarrhea, vomiting; peaks within 48 to 72 h after heroin
2Urgent risks
BreathingPinpoint pupils, slow breathing, decreased consciousness
Breathing can fail again within hours as the reversal agent wears off

If the opioid overdose triad is present, choose naloxone, with bag-mask breaths until it works; intubation is rarely needed when naloxone is given quickly.

AlcoholSeizures at 12 to 48 h; disorientation, hallucinations, fever, usually at 48 to 96 h
Delirium tremens: mortality 1% to 5%

If it is delirium tremens, choose an intravenous benzodiazepine, promptly.

SedativeBenzodiazepine stopped after long-term use
Potentially life-threatening, like alcohol withdrawal

If an outpatient dependent on a benzodiazepine must come off it, choose a slow taper of a long-acting benzodiazepine.

HeartChest pain with agitation after cocaine
Evaluate as any possible ischemia; beta-blockers are contraindicated

If there is cardiovascular toxicity or agitation, choose a benzodiazepine first; nitrates or an alpha-blocker if chest pain or hypertension persists.

HeatHyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis or seizures with PCP or a stimulant

If agitation is driving the heat, choose benzodiazepine sedation; with a stimulant, also external cooling (ice bath or evaporative).

ReversalOversedated long-term benzodiazepine user
In long-term users, reversal may precipitate withdrawal and occasionally seizures

If the user is long-term, choose supportive care of airway, breathing and circulation; no flumazenil.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Opioid overdoseDecreased consciousness, slow breathingPinpoint pupils with slow breathing; reverses with naloxone
Sedative overdoseSlurred speech, ataxia, decreased alertness Alcohol intoxicationAlcohol intoxication looks alike: typically depressed central nervous system function and impaired motor skills.Normal-size pupils, even when breathing is slow
Inhalant intoxicationIncoordination, unsteadiness, lethargyClears quickly after use Inhalant cluesBoys 14 to 17 are at highest risk. Effects typically last 15 to 45 minutes and may include loss of consciousness. Liver tests may rise with repeated use. Chronic nitrous oxide: vitamin B12 deficiency with polyneuropathy.
Opioid withdrawalDilated pupils, autonomic overactivityFrom 4 h after heroin, slower after methadone; yawning, runny nose, goose flesh, diarrhea
Cocaine or amphetamineAgitation, sweating, tachycardia; chronic methamphetamine: skin sores, decayed teeth MethamphetamineHeavy use causes weight loss, sores from skin picking, and decayed or cracked teeth ("meth mouth") from grinding and a dry mouth. Fleeting visual or tactile hallucinations (bugs under the skin) favor a drug-induced psychosis: rule out the drug before diagnosing mania or schizophrenia.Dilated pupils, hypertension, hyperthermia; can bring coronary ischemia CocaethyleneTaken with alcohol, cocaine forms cocaethylene, which prolongs and strengthens its sympathomimetic effects.; cocaine lasts under 1 hour, amphetamine several hours
Dilated pupils, fever, fast pulse, deliriumDry, warm skin; urinary retention; ileus; no sweating Causes and cautionsTricyclics (such as doxepin), clozapine and some antihistamines, alone or combined. Get an electrocardiogram (ECG) early (step 4); a tricyclic overdose can widen the QRS complex (treatment: Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity). No haloperidol: it adds anticholinergic effect. Normal muscle tone argues against neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
PCPViolence, hallucinations, delusions, hypertensionNystagmus in any direction, vertical included PCPConfusion, dissociation, ataxia and a high pain tolerance.
Alcoholic hallucinosisAuditory, tactile or visual hallucinationsUsually 12 to 48 h; clear sensorium, autonomic signs usually absent
Delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal delirium) In a vignetteHallucinations: Get them off me!Confusion, fleeting hallucinations, tremor, sweating, fever, fast pulseUsually 48 to 96 h; disorientation with autonomic instability; mortality 1% to 5%
Benzodiazepine withdrawalLike alcohol withdrawal; potentially life-threatening1 to 2 days (short-acting) or several days to a week (long-acting) after stopping
Stimulant withdrawalLong sleep, hunger, low mood, unpleasant dreams after a bingeA crash, not arousal; the depression can bring suicide attempts
Cannabis FDA labelLegal prescription use: the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) label covers adults with anorexia and weight loss in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), and chemotherapy nausea and vomiting after standard antiemetics fail.Fast pulse, red conjunctivae, hunger, dry mouth, slowed timeRed conjunctivae with hunger; hyperemesis (cyclical vomiting usually eased by warm showers) is a separate picture
Primary psychotic disorderDelusions or hallucinations, which PCP also causesPersists about 1 month or longer after intoxication or withdrawal ends, or began before use
Agitation and high arousal, as with a stimulantA stimulant adds dilated pupils, sweating, tachycardia and hypertension
4Workup

Name the drug and whether it is intoxication or withdrawal, then treat by drug (step 7).

Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Vertical or rotary nystagmus with violencePCPIntravenous or intramuscular benzodiazepine
Seizure 12 to 48 h after the last drink In practiceSome references (eg, MSD Manual) give 6 to 48 hours.Alcohol withdrawal seizureBenzodiazepine; routine phenytoin unlikely to help
First seizure after 2 days of missed doses of a medicine taken for anxiety or sleep; no seizure history Seizure on stopping versus on the drugBupropion and tricyclic antidepressants can cause dose-dependent seizures while being taken; seizures are not associated with their withdrawal. Stopping paroxetine or venlafaxine gives a discontinuation syndrome (dysphoria, fatigue, dizziness, gastrointestinal upset, flu-like symptoms) without seizures.Withdrawal from a short-acting benzodiazepine such as alprazolam; can appear as early as 24 hoursTreat as benzodiazepine withdrawal; prevent it with a longer-acting drug tapered over weeks to months
Drinks nightly to fall asleep, then wakes during the night; macrocytosis; AST at least twice ALT LimitsMore than 7 drinks a week or 3 a day for women and for men 65 or older; more than 14 a week or 4 a day for men under 65Alcohol use disorder: awakening as the alcohol level fallsScreen for alcohol use disorder rather than treating insomnia alone
Vomiting, diarrhea, poor sleep and muscle aches, with normal pulse, blood pressure and temperatureOpioid withdrawal; alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal typically raises the vital signsTreat the withdrawal (step 7); fever or confusion points to another cause
New energy drinks through the day; anxiety, insomnia, tremor, palpitations, raised blood pressureCaffeine intoxicationSubstance-induced comes first: not panic or adjustment disorder; alcohol withdrawal is usually associated with heavy drinking, and light drinking is very unlikely to cause it; no elevated mood or grandiosity, so not hypomania
Party drug, alone or with an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor); hyperthermia, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, a seizure with low sodiumMDMA (methylenedioxymethamphetamine, ecstasy) intoxication with serotonin syndrome Urine screenSynthetic amphetamines and analogues, such as MDMA, may not show up as amphetamines on routine urine toxicology screens.An amphetamine plus serotonin toxicity; hyponatremia from fluid intake and antidiuretic hormone release brings the seizure
Seizure in pregnancy with agitation, sweating, dilated pupils, low sodium, no proteinuria and a normal head CTAmphetamine intoxication, not eclampsiaUrine drug testing confirms it; telling it from eclampsia may decide whether emergency delivery is needed
Pause point
Altered patient, ingestion unknown Offered: naloxone Normal-size pupils and normal breathing → Supportive care while the toxidrome is read; naloxone is for pinpoint pupils with slow breathing
Chest pain and hypertension after cocaine Offered: a beta-blocker Beta-blockers are contraindicated in cocaine toxicity → A benzodiazepine first; nitrates or an alpha-blocker if chest pain or hypertension persists
Confused, sweating and tachycardic days after the last drink Offered as alcoholic hallucinosis Disorientation with autonomic instability; hallucinosis keeps a clear sensorium → Delirium tremens: a benzodiazepine, thiamine before glucose
Agitated patient, urine screen pending Offered: waiting on the screen before treating The toxidrome is read at the bedside; routine screens often miss synthetic cathinones → Treat the toxidrome now
5Diagnostic criteria
7Treatment
1

Reversethe opioid overdose triad

Naloxone, with bag-mask breaths until it works

The reversal agent can wear off before the opioid, so observe; it can precipitate withdrawal. Given quickly, it rarely leaves a need for intubation.

2

1st lineagitation from PCP, cocaine or amphetamine

A benzodiazepine, intravenous or intramuscular

Lowers central sympathetic outflow. For cocaine, nitrates or an alpha-blocker if chest pain or hypertension persists after this first drug. Guideline detailLorazepam 2 to 4 mg or diazepam 5 to 10 mg, intravenous or intramuscular

3

1st linemoderate to severe alcohol withdrawal

A benzodiazepine, dosed by withdrawal scale score

Guideline detailCIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised) or SAWS (Short Alcohol Withdrawal Scale) scores set the as-needed doses Long-acting chlordiazepoxide or diazepam; in the hospital, intravenous lorazepam; with cirrhosis or alcoholic hepatitis, lorazepam or oxazepam, whose glucuronidation liver disease spares. Also for seizures (not routine phenytoin) and, intravenously and promptly, delirium tremens; Why notAntipsychotics may lower the seizure threshold, already low in alcohol withdrawal.. With intravenous fluids, thiamine before glucose. Guideline detail100 mg intravenously, before any glucose

4

1st lineopioid withdrawal

Buprenorphine or methadone

Distressing, not dangerous, after a spontaneous stop. Start buprenorphine only once withdrawal signs are clear: a partial agonist given while a full agonist is still on board displaces it and precipitates withdrawal. Guideline detailSublingual buprenorphine 4 to 12 mg to start, an alternative to methadone

5

Adjunctautonomic signs

Clonidine

Can ease autonomic signs, such as blood pressure, in opioid withdrawal; in alcohol withdrawal only as an adjunct to a benzodiazepine.

6

Avoidtempting but wrong

Flumazenil in a long-term user; urinary acidification for PCP; beta-blockers in cocaine toxicity

Guideline detailFlumazenil is best kept for respiratory depression during a procedure.

First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
PCP agitationBenzodiazepine; a rapid-acting antipsychotic second lineNo urinary acidification: acidosis, myoglobin in the kidney
Opioid withdrawalBuprenorphine or methadoneNot naloxone: it treats overdose
Benzodiazepine withdrawalSlow outpatient taper of a long-acting one (eg clonazepam)Can last weeks
Stimulant withdrawalAssess suicide riskIn some users the depression is prolonged and drives relapse
Cannabinoid hyperemesisStop cannabisWarm showers usually relieve it
Supportive care; a benzodiazepine for agitation or seizures; sodium bicarbonate for a QRS over 100 msNo haloperidol; no physostigmine with a tricyclic
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
After naloxoneObserve until its effect is gone; breathing can fail again within hours
Alcohol withdrawal under wayKeep dosing by symptom score; watch for delirium tremens (step 5)
Psychosis lasts about 1 month after stopping Consider an independent psychotic disorder
Active use, intoxication or withdrawal Count it as a modifiable suicide risk factor; complete the risk assessment once sober, under close observation until then
Long-term care after withdrawal
Use disorderChooseWatch for
Other drugsNot relapse drugs for alcohol: bupropion and varenicline (smoking cessation), fomepizole (antidote for methanol or ethylene glycol).Naltrexone or acamprosate, both first lineNaltrexone helps most who take it consistently; not with acute hepatitis, liver failure or opioid use: choose acamprosate then, unless kidney impairment is significant
Naltrexone: it can start while drinking continuesNot disulfiram: abstinent patients only
Acamprosate, used to maintain abstinenceEach drug's own limits: the Alcohol row above
Disulfiram, best in highly motivated patients, after 48 hours of abstinenceDrinking on it: flushing, throbbing headache, tachycardia Disulfiram reactionHeavy drinking may add vomiting and hypotension; effects may last 3 to 7 days after the last dose.
Alcohol, alongside eitherAlcoholics Anonymous; motivational psychotherapy TherapyTherapy also teaches avoiding the situations that set off drinking.
StimulantCBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) to prevent relapse; an antipsychotic for psychosisNo drug has proven consistently effective
Buprenorphine or methadone maintenance, the standard of care over withdrawal management aloneLowers relapse and fatal overdose
Can be prescribed in an officeStart only once withdrawal is clear, or it precipitates withdrawal In practice:Low-dose starts give small, rising buprenorphine doses while the full agonist continues, to avoid precipitated withdrawal.
Only through a licensed opioid treatment programQTc (the heart-rate-corrected Q-to-T interval) prolongation and torsades: ECG at start and during titration
Long-acting naltrexone, from an opioid-free stateOnly after at least 7 days without a full dose of another opioid agonist
Practice
  1. 26-year-old man brought by police after fighting strangers in the street shouting that he cannot be hurt; eyes jerk up and down T 38.4 °C · BP 170/104 mm Hg · HR 118/min · pupils midsize · respirations 18/min → Intravenous lorazepam → violent agitation, vertical nystagmus and hypertension suggest PCP; benzodiazepines are the preferred sedative; urinary acidification is no longer recommended, and normal breathing with midsize pupils is not an opioid picture
  2. 29-year-old woman with chest pain an hour after a party restless, talking fast; skin wet with sweat pupils 7 mm, reactive · BP 182/106 mm Hg · HR 132/min · T 38.0 °C · no nystagmus → Cocaine intoxication → agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, dilated pupils and sweating form the sympathomimetic picture, and cocaine can trigger coronary ischemia; heroin gives small pupils and slow breathing; cannabis raises the pulse, but its picture is red eyes, hunger and a dry mouth rather than sweating with dilated pupils
  3. 34-year-old man with chest pain and agitation after using cocaine ECG (electrocardiogram): sinus tachycardia, no ST-segment elevation; troponin pending BP 176/102 mm Hg · HR 128/min · pupils dilated · diaphoretic · oxygen saturation 98% → An intravenous benzodiazepine → benzodiazepines are first-line for cocaine agitation and cardiovascular toxicity; beta-blockers such as metoprolol are contraindicated in cocaine toxicity, because they leave alpha stimulation unopposed, which can worsen coronary vasoconstriction; naloxone treats opioid overdose, not a stimulant
  4. 22-year-old man found unresponsive in a restroom a needle and spoon beside him; shallow, snoring respirations; no response to voice respirations 6/min · oxygen saturation 84% · pupils 1 mm · BP 104/68 mm Hg · T 36.4 °C → Naloxone → pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and decreased consciousness are the opioid triad; naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, is not routine and can provoke seizures; lorazepam would deepen the respiratory depression
  5. 55-year-old man admitted for pancreatitis; last drink 60 hours ago now disoriented, says rats run across the floor, drenched in sweat T 38.1 °C · HR 126/min · BP 168/98 mm Hg · coarse tremor → Delirium tremens → disorientation, visual hallucinations, fever, sweating and tachycardia, usually within 48 to 96 hours, are delirium tremens, which can be fatal; hallucinosis (usually 12 to 48 hours) leaves the sensorium clear and the vital signs usually normal, and opioid withdrawal after a spontaneous stop is not life-threatening
  6. 48-year-old woman 20 hours after her last drink tremulous, anxious, sweating; symptom scale score moderate needs intravenous fluids for vomiting HR 112/min · BP 152/94 mm Hg · glucose 92 mg/dL → Benzodiazepine; thiamine before glucose → benzodiazepines are first-line for moderate alcohol withdrawal, and with intravenous fluids thiamine goes before glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; clonidine is only an adjunct to a benzodiazepine
  7. 31-year-old man who stopped heroin 1 day ago yawning, runny nose, goose flesh, cramps and diarrhea wants to stop using pupils 6 mm · HR 104/min · BP 142/88 mm Hg · T 37.2 °C → Buprenorphine → opioid withdrawal after a spontaneous stop is distressing but not life-threatening; buprenorphine or methadone treats it, and clonidine can help; naloxone, an opioid antagonist, treats overdose, not withdrawal
  8. 24-year-old man with 6 months of repeated bouts of vomiting smokes cannabis daily; feels better only under hot showers normal between bouts HR 96/min · abdomen soft · lipase normal · T 36.9 °C → Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome → cyclical vomiting relieved with warm showers in daily cannabis use, which resolves with cessation; the cannabis use is the clue the other labels ignore
  9. 52-year-old man brought in confused, picking at the air shouts that bugs crawl on him calls the nurses flight attendants Well last week, says his sister; toxicology negative T 37.9 °C · HR 118/min · BP 162/100 mm Hg · palmar erythema, gynecomastia → Delirium tremens → severe confusion, disorientation, visual hallucinations and autonomic instability are delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal delirium); palmar erythema and gynecomastia are signs of chronic alcohol use even when no drinking is reported, and brief psychotic disorder does not present with abnormal vital signs
Pairs with Delirium: is a withdrawal driving the confusion? Psychosis: did the psychosis start during or soon after use?
Transferable rule

Pupils and breathing first: small pupils with slow breathing is an opioid; big pupils with sweating and a fast pulse is a stimulant or opioid withdrawal, while big pupils with dry, hot skin is an anticholinergic drug; nystagmus with violence is PCP.
